questions.q: What is the article's main argument?
options: The 2001 anthrax attacks led to a fully modernized national biosecurity network
Post-2001 biodefense systems have stagnated, leaving the U.S. vulnerable
BioWatch has been upgraded repeatedly and now detects threats within hours
Federal agencies coordinated well after 2001, but funding cuts ended the plan
questions.explain: Experts say systems built after 2001 are outdated and the federal response underfunded and uncoordinated.

questions.q: What did Robert Stevens find in the envelope at his office?
options: A routine tabloid tip with a photograph attached
A package of newspapers and mail for the office staff
A letter containing a grainy white powder
A plain envelope with a harmless sample of film
questions.explain: Stevens opened an envelope containing a letter and a grainy white powder and later developed inhalation anthrax.

questions.q: How long is the delay between sample collection and identification with BioWatch?
options: About one week
12 to 36 hours
3 to 5 days
1 to 2 hours
questions.explain: Workers must manually collect samples and bring them to a lab, causing a 12 to 36 hour delay.

questions.q: What did federal investigators ultimately conclude about the 2001 anthrax attacks?
options: They were carried out by a single perpetrator who was a biodefense researcher
They were the result of a coordinated international terror cell
They were traced to an accidental release from a public vaccine factory
They were caused by contaminated consumer products mailed nationwide
questions.explain: Investigators tied the attacks after nearly a decade to a single perpetrator, a biodefense researcher.

questions.q: Why do experts say an intentional attack may be more likely now?
options: Anthrax spores are now sold openly through commercial laboratories
Federal agencies have stopped sharing intelligence about bioterror
AI and gene-editing make it easier to engineer pathogens
Detection systems have been scaled back at airports and ports
questions.explain: Advances in AI, synthetic biology and gene-editing make it easier for bad actors to engineer pathogens.
